query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of base elements in a refractory MoNbTaW high-entropy alloy with aluminum will enable the formation of a stable Al2O3 surface layer during elevated-temperature oxidation in air, significantly reducing oxygen uptake compared to the same alloy without Al doping.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline equimolar MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy, prepared by arc melting and homogenized in vacuum.
generation.intervention: Replace a fraction of the base elements with aluminum (e.g., 8 at% Al) during the alloy’s initial melt, accompanied by a homogenization heat treatment.
generation.conditions: Subject the Al-containing alloy to 1200 °C in a flowing oxygen-rich environment (e.g., air) for up to 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: An external protective alumina (Al2O3) film formed by selective oxidation of aluminum at high temperature.
generation.mechanism: The added aluminum preferentially oxidizes to form a continuous, dense Al2O3 surface layer, which inhibits further oxygen penetration and slows subsequent internal oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under these test conditions, the Al-doped alloy will exhibit a markedly lower mass gain (on the order of at least 30% reduction) and less spallation than an identical undoped reference alloy.
generation.baseline: An otherwise-identical MoNbTaW alloy without aluminum shows higher weight gain and less protective oxide layers at similar temperatures.
generation.boundary: Excessive aluminum additions or large thermal cycling could degrade oxide adherence; effectiveness may vary for other refractory element ratios or lower/higher temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of oxidation resistance improvement depends on the Al content, processing route, and specific atmosphere.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of MoNbTaW-based alloys via arc melting in vacuum: one undoped and one with 8 at% Al substitution. Homogenize both under identical thermal schedules. Expose coupons from both sets to 1200 °C in air for 100 hours.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional oxide characterization via SEM and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped samples do not show at least a 30% decrease in mass gain or fail to form a stable alumina-rich oxide layer relative to the undoped samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties.
